ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: in the figure, two parallel metal guide rails MN and PQ are placed along the direction of the inclined plane, and the angle between the guide-rail plane and the horizontal plane is marked as θ; metal rod ab is on the left side and cd is on the right side, and both are bridged between the two guide rails and perpendicular to the guide rails. In the figure, an external force F upward along the inclined plane is drawn on cd, and the magnetic field B is marked as upward perpendicular to the guide-rail plane. Then reason: before the light rope is burned through, both rods are stationary, there is no induced current, and therefore they are not subject to Ampere force. Take ab, cd, and the light rope as a whole; in the direction along the inclined plane the external forces balance: upward is F, downward is the component of total gravity (2m+m)g sinθ=3mg sinθ, so F=3mg sinθ. After the light rope is burned through, F remains unchanged. Take the two metal rods as one system; the resultant external force in the direction along the inclined plane is F-3mg sinθ=0; the guide rails are smooth and frictionless, and the support force is perpendicular to the inclined plane; the currents in the two rods are the same, and the Ampere forces they receive are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so for the two-rod system the resultant force is zero. Therefore the momentum of the system in the direction along the inclined plane is conserved. Initially the velocities of both rods are 0, so at any moment in the direction along the inclined plane there is: 2m·v_ab_signed + m·v_cd_signed = 0. From this it can be known that the two rods move in opposite directions, and the magnitudes of the speeds satisfy 2m v_ab = m v_cd, that is, v_ab∶v_cd=1∶2.
